theme: Greater than Moses; the Sabbath rest remains
readingInstruction: Read Hebrews 3:1-4:13. This is a long reading with a single theme: the danger of an unbelieving heart and the promise of God’s rest. Keep your finger on the repeated phrase from Psalm 95, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” It appears three times, and each time it presses on the reader.
settingTheScene: Having shown that the Son is greater than angels, the author now compares him with Moses. For a Jewish audience, this was the more sensitive comparison. Moses was the lawgiver, the faithful servant, the man who spoke with God face to face. To suggest anyone is greater than Moses was bold. But the point is not to diminish Moses. It is to show that Moses himself pointed forward. Then the author turns to the wilderness generation, those who were delivered from Egypt but failed to enter the promised land because of unbelief. The warning is plain: do not follow their example. The promise of rest is still open.
observation: Jesus is called the “apostle and high priest of our confession” (3:1). He is both sent from God and sent to God on our behalf.
Moses was faithful “as a servant in all God’s house,” but Christ is faithful “as a son over God’s house” (3:5-6).
The house is built by God, and “we are his house if indeed we hold fast our confidence” (3:6).
Psalm 95:7-11 is quoted at length and applied to the readers: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (3:7-8).
The wilderness generation died because of unbelief and disobedience (3:16-19).
“A promise remains” of entering God’s rest (4:1), and the readers are told to strive to enter it (4:11).
The gospel was preached to the wilderness generation, but it did not benefit them because they were not united by faith with those who listened (4:2).
The word of God is described as living, active, and sharper than a two-edged sword, discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart (4:12-13).
interpretation:
The comparison with Moses is one of respect and fulfillment. Both Moses and Jesus were faithful to God’s house, but they hold different positions. Moses was a servant in the house, and he served well. Jesus is the Son over the house, and in fact the builder of it. A house is always inferior to its builder, and a servant is always inferior to the son. This is not a criticism of Moses but a recognition that Moses’ faithful service was itself a testimony pointing forward to someone greater. Numbers 12:7 calls Moses faithful in all God’s house. Hebrews says: yes, and now the Son has come.

The conditional phrase in 3:6 deserves attention: “we are his house if indeed we hold fast our confidence.” This is the first appearance of a theme that runs through Hebrews. The author is not suggesting that believers earn their place in God’s house by perseverance. Rather, perseverance is how true faith shows itself. Those who belong to Christ will hold fast to him, and the warnings are God’s means of keeping them holding on.

Next the author reaches into Psalm 95 and applies it to his readers. The wilderness generation saw God’s mighty works. They were rescued from Egypt, fed with manna, and guided by the cloud. And yet they rebelled and tested God. The author’s diagnosis is clear: “an evil, unbelieving heart” that leads to falling away from the living God. The remedy is just as clear: exhort one another every day, as long as it is called “today,” so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. Notice that the remedy is communal. Faith is not a private possession but something we guard together.

Chapter 4 develops the idea of rest. In Genesis 2, God rested on the seventh day. In Joshua, Israel entered the land. But Psalm 95, written centuries after Joshua, still speaks of a rest to enter “today.” The author’s reasoning is that if Joshua had given them the final rest, David would not have spoken of another day. Therefore “there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God.” The rest is the fullness of salvation, communion with God, and relief from striving to earn his favor. It is entered by faith, and it is fully enjoyed when Christ returns. We enter it now in part by trusting his finished work, and we will enter it fully in the new creation.

The urgency of verse 11, “Let us strive to enter that rest,” sounds paradoxical. How do you strive to rest? The answer is that you strive against unbelief. The effort is to keep trusting, to keep coming back to Christ, and to refuse to harden your heart.

The section ends with a vivid picture of the word of God. It is living, active, and piercing. It exposes our hearts. Nothing is hidden from the one with whom we have to do. This is frightening if we are hiding, but it is also the basis for confidence, because the God who sees everything is the one who has provided a high priest.
connection: The Moses comparison draws on Numbers 12 and Exodus 33:11, where Moses speaks with God face to face. The warning from Psalm 95 looks back to the rebellions at Massah and Meribah (Exodus 17, Numbers 14), which you read earlier in this plan. The theme of rest links Genesis 2:2, Exodus 20:8-11, Deuteronomy 12:9-10, and Joshua 21:44. Jesus himself offers this rest in Matthew 11:28-30. The living word of 4:12 echoes Isaiah 55:10-11 and prepares for the high priest passage that immediately follows.
application:
First, take the word “today” seriously. If you have been delaying obedience or repentance, today is the day to hear his voice. Choose one thing you know the Lord is asking of you, and do it.

Second, ask whether you are keeping up the daily exhortation Hebrews commands. Who is encouraging you in the faith? Who are you encouraging? If no one, take a first step this week toward someone in your church.

Third, think about rest. Many believers live as if salvation depends on constant effort. The Sabbath rest that remains is in part the rest of knowing that Christ has finished the work. Let your weekly rest day be a regular practice of trusting that.

Fourth, let Hebrews 4:12 shape how you read Scripture. Bring your heart to the word, expecting it to read you.
prayerPrompts: Tell God that today you hear his voice, and ask him to soften your heart.
Confess where you have hardened your heart.
Thank him for the rest that remains.
